sections.history: Ayyarmalai, also spelled Iyermalai, rises from the plain on the southern bank of the Kaveri in Karur district, a few kilometres from Kulithalai. In the Tevaram the place is called Thiruvatpokki, and the saint Appar sang its praise, with Sundarar also credited by some accounts. It is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of Chola Nadu, the shrines on the southern side of the river. The exact age of the present buildings is not firmly documented: worship here is understood to reach back to the Tevaram age, while the stone structures are generally thought to be medieval and were added to in later centuries. A custom of bringing water from the Kaveri up the hill for the daily anointing of the Lord is said to have been kept by the temple's servitors for a very long time.
sections.architecture: The temple sits on the summit and is reached by a long flight of stone steps, broken by resting mandapas with carved pillars; counts of the steps vary, with figures of around nine hundred and fifty given by one reckoning. At the top the sanctum of Ratnagiriswarar holds a Shiva linga honoured as self-manifested, said to have appeared among a ring of rocks. The Lord faces west, while the goddess Surumbar Kuzhali has her own shrine facing east, an arrangement uncommon among Shiva temples. A pillared hall at the temple takes the living rock of the hill into its design, so that stone and sanctuary seem to grow from one another. The sacred tree of the shrine is the neem.
sections.legends: The name Vatpokki is explained by a tradition from this hill. A king, it is told, came here in search of gems. Shiva appeared to him as a Brahmin and asked that a vessel be filled with water from the Kaveri. When the task proved impossible and the king, in anger, raised his sword, the Lord stayed the blow and instead gave him a precious stone. In Tamil, vaal is the sword and pokki the one who turns it aside, and the name Ratnagiriswarar, Lord of the Jewel Hill, is said to recall the gift. A second tradition holds that the hill is a fragment of the mythic Mount Meru, torn away when the wind god Vayu contended with the serpent Adishesha and flung down here.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great night of the temple, when devotees climb in numbers to keep vigil on the hill. The monthly Pradosham is observed here as at every Shiva temple, along with the annual festivals of the Tamil calendar common to the shrines of the Kaveri country. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar and the specific rites vary from year to year.
sections.experience: Ayyarmalai asks something of the pilgrim, and rewards it. Begin the climb early, before the sun is strong, pausing at the resting halls as generations of devotees have done. From the summit the green Kaveri plain spreads out below, and in the sanctum the west-facing Lord and the east-facing goddess are seen in a quiet that the climb has earned. Many pilgrims make a day of it by first visiting Kadambavaneswarar at Kulithalai in the morning, then coming up this hill, and ending at the hill shrine of Thiruvengoimalai in the evening.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days. Plan the climb for the cooler hours.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the foot of the hill, so comfortable shoes are best kept for the road.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted on the stairway and in the outer areas but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Ayyarmalai lies about 10 km from the Kulithalai bus stand in Karur district, on the Karur–Tiruchirappalli side of the Kaveri. Kulithalai has a railway station on the Tiruchirappalli–Karur line, and Tiruchirappalli, with the nearest airport, is roughly 40 km away. Local buses and autos serve the foot of the hill.
